<reason>Both sides were disciplined and vivid. PRO's frame (harm clusters at dispersal; restrictions displace drinking into unsupervised settings; equity for night workers) was memorably argued and its pressure question forced CON to concede a timed transit "exit pulse," which PRO exploited well ("my policy with a stopwatch attached"). But CON pre-empted and then cleanly held the distinguishing line the motion itself invites: transit that empties a closed district serves last call, whereas transit running so venues can keep pouring serves the extra round — and the motion asks what a city relies on *mainly*. CON also landed the sharpest single hit of the debate: PRO explicitly declined to claim a shorter night, so CON's "the extra hour is not a substitution, it is the pre-load plus more doubles on top" left PRO's total-harm-per-unit-nightlife metric exposed, and PRO's answer (price, satiation, refusal of service) was thin, especially after CON noted refusal of service is weakest when the room is fullest. CON also gave a real mechanism against migration (last-entry friction, cost/space/risk of hosting) and a plausible account of Sydney as a leaky single-precinct rule; PRO's repeated closing claim that CON "never named the mechanism" therefore misdescribes the record and weakens PRO's crystallization. PRO retains a live route on supervision-versus-unsupervision and on the unavoidable dispersal moment, but CON answered that directly — hours of pouring change how large and drunk the surge is — and framed the final comparison more accurately against the proposition as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange around PRO's forced admission: CON's question "what stops the extra rounds — or do you concede the night gets larger and drunker?" drew PRO's "I'm not claiming the night gets shorter," which CON converted into the decisive comparison that the extra hour is pre-load plus more doubles, not the same alcohol relocated to a safer room. Paired with CON's defense that an exit pulse timed to closing is not the proposition, this blunted PRO's strongest concession trap.</best_rebuttal>
